title: Finding What's Eating Resources
intro: A server feels slow. Before touching anything else, you need to know what's actually consuming CPU, memory, and disk.

steps.explanation: 6.9G used out of 7.8G — this box is nearly out of memory.
steps.why: -h prints human-readable units (G/M) instead of raw kilobytes — the numbers are identical either way, but you shouldn't have to do division in your head during an incident.

steps.prompt: List running processes sorted to find the biggest resource users.
steps.fake_output:
USER  PID  %CPU  %MEM  COMMAND
root  4821  95.2  42.1  node server.js
root  1023   2.1   1.5  sshd
steps.explanation: That node process is using 95% CPU and 42% memory — clearly the culprit.
steps.why: 'top' updates live and is better for watching a process's usage change in real time; 'ps aux' gives you a single static snapshot you can pipe into grep/sort/scripts — pick based on whether you need to watch or just capture.

steps.prompt: Check disk space too, since resource issues often come in pairs.
steps.explanation: 96% disk usage — worth checking what's filling it, often log files.
steps.why: 'df' reports space at the filesystem level; it won't tell you WHICH files are responsible for that usage — that's what the next step (du) is for. df answers 'is this the problem,' du answers 'what's causing it.'

steps.prompt: Find what's taking up space in /var/log.
steps.explanation: A 2.1G log file that was never rotated — a very common real-world cause of disk pressure.
steps.why: -s summarizes each argument to one total instead of listing every file/subdirectory recursively — without it, du -h /var/log/* would print a noisy line for every single file inside every subfolder, burying the one number you actually care about.
